Hinged Ptolemy

GeometryCirclesTriangles
Game: Four dots sit on a circle and a triangle swings around one of them to show that two sums of lengths are always equal.
How to play: Drag dots A, B, C or P, or focus one and use the arrow keys. Move Rotation to turn the triangle, tick Show names, or press Reset.
0%
Look for the math

Ptolemy's theorem looks like a sum of products, but this picture turns it into two ordinary triangles. Drag the dots and move the slider: the two numbers under the picture stay the same.

Four points on one circle

Go round the circle in the order A, B, P, C. The two lines AC and BP cross as diagonals of a cyclic quadrilateral. Ptolemy's theorem claims

AC·BP + AB·CP = AP·BC.

The test checks this for thousands of groups of four points in the right order around the circle, with all four dots on the same circle. It holds up to rounding; reorder the dots and the matching of sides changes, so the order matters.

The hinge at A

The slider turns triangle ACP about A through the angle from AC to AB. A rotation keeps every length, so AC' = AC and C'P' = CP. At a full turn C' lies on the ray AB. Because ABPC is cyclic, the angle at C is the supplement of the angle ABP; after the turn the angle AC'P' equals that same supplement, so C'P' ∥ BP.

Two pairs of similar triangles

Let P'' be where the line AP' meets BP. Triangles ABP'' and AC'P' are similar, giving

BP'' = AB·C'P'/AC' = AB·CP/AC.

Triangles ABC and AP''P are similar too, so PP'' = BC·AP/AC. Since P'' sits on the segment from B to P at a full turn, PP'' = BP + BP''. Multiply by AC and Ptolemy's identity falls out. The logic test checks both length formulas and the sum over many positions of the four dots.

What the slider really does

The old scrollbar ran from 0 to 105 and was divided by 100. Below 100 only part of the turn has happened, so C'P' is not parallel to BP; at 100 the proof lines up; past 100 the hinge swings beyond B. The page also says P' lands on the extension of BP when ABC is an equilateral or isosceles triangle. The test finds that this is true precisely when AB = AC — the two sides meeting at the hinge — and false for an isosceles triangle whose equal sides meet at B or at C.

Set Rotation to 100, tick Show names, then drag P: the yellow points move but C'P' stays parallel to BP and the two numbers in the status line stay equal.
